verses.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,
“Send men, that they may spy out the land of Canaan, which I give to the children of Israel. Of every tribe of their fathers, you shall send a man, every one a prince among them.”
Moses sent them from the wilderness of Paran according to the commandment of Yahweh. All them were men who were heads of the children of Israel.
These were their names: Of the tribe of Reuben, Shammua the son of Zaccur.
Of the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat the son of Hori.
Of the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh.
Of the tribe of Issachar, Igal the son of Joseph.
Of the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Nun.
Of the tribe of Benjamin, Palti the son of Raphu.
Of the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel the son of Sodi.
Of the tribe of Joseph, of the tribe of Manasseh, Gaddi the son of Susi.
Of the tribe of Dan, Ammiel the son of Gemalli.
Of the tribe of Asher, Sethur the son of Michael.
Of the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi the son of Vophsi.
Of the tribe of Gad, Geuel the son of Machi.
These are the names of the men who Moses sent to spy out the land. Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun Joshua.
Moses sent them to spy out the land of Canaan, and said to them, “Go up this way by the South, and go up into the hill country.
See the land, what it is; and the people who dwell therein, whether they are strong or weak, whether they are few or many;
and what the land is that they dwell in, whether it is good or bad; and what cities they are that they dwell in, whether in camps, or in strongholds;
and what the land is, whether it is fat or lean, whether there is wood therein, or not. Be courageous, and bring some of the fruit of the land.” Now the time was the time of the first-ripe grapes.
So they went up, and spied out the land from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob, to the entrance of Hamath.
They went up by the South, and came to Hebron; and Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were there. (Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)
They came to the valley of Eshcol, and cut down from there a branch with one cluster of grapes, and they bore it on a staff between two. They also brought some of the pomegranates and figs.
That place was called the valley of Eshcol, because of the cluster which the children of Israel cut down from there.
They returned from spying out the land at the end of forty days.

They went and came to Moses, to Aaron, and to all the congregation of the children of Israel, to the wilderness of Paran, to Kadesh; and brought back word to them and to all the congregation. They showed them the fruit of the land.
They told him, and said, “We came to the land where you sent us. Surely it flows with milk and honey, and this is its fruit.
However the people who dwell in the land are strong, and the cities are fortified and very large. Moreover, we saw the children of Anak there.
Amalek dwells in the land of the South. The Hittite, the Jebusite, and the Amorite dwell in the hill country. The Canaanite dwells by the sea, and along the side of the Jordan.”
Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, “Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!”
But the men who went up with him said, “We aren’t able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we.”

They brought up an evil report of the land which they had spied out to the children of Israel, saying, “The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land that eats up its inhabitants; and all the people who we saw in it are men of great stature.
There we saw the Nephilim,  the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim.  We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.”

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks to Moses—just as He always does when it matters most. It's not the destination that concerns Him first, but whether His people will listen and trust His voice along the way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: See what the Lord is careful about here? He says *I give* the land, not 'I will try to give' or 'if you're strong enough.' The promise is already His to give—the spying is meant to steady faith, not to settle the matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses sends them from Paran, the wilderness where the people have been waiting. Notice: these are heads, princes—the very men the congregation will look to when the report comes back. Everything hinges on their hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve names. Twelve tribes. One man from each. Most I don't hear of again—they faded into the unbelief that came later. Only two names endure: Caleb and Joshua (who here is still called Hoshea). The Lord remembers those who trust Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There it is—Moses renames Hoshea 'Joshua,' meaning 'The Lord is salvation.' A name is a prophecy, a calling. In the dark hour when fear speaks loudest, this man will remember his true name and what it means.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses gives them clear orders: go up South, climb to the hill country, and *observe*. See the land, see the people, see whether the cities are camps or strongholds. He wants honest assessment—not to cancel the promise, but to know what faith will need to overcome.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He tells them to be courageous and bring back fruit. Fat or lean land, timber or not—details matter. And look—it's grape season. In the abundance the Lord has already shown them, He invites them to see His provision.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They traverse the whole length of the land—from Zin to Rehob, from south to north. The scope of their survey is enormous. They see the whole inheritance, every corner the Lord is about to give.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hebron, where giants dwell. And that aside—that Hebron was built seven years before Zoan—isn't mere trivia. It's a father's way of saying: 'Look, reader. This place has been ancient and fortified for ages. Can you see why ten of us will be afraid?'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One cluster of grapes so large they had to carry it on a staff between two men. Pomegranates. Figs. The abundance is real, visible, tangible. But will they trust what they can see?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eshcol means 'cluster.' The place takes its name from the evidence of plenty. Names tell the truth about what the Lord does—the land itself testifies to His abundance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty days. Long enough to see clearly, to gather evidence, to know the truth. And when they return, what will they choose to remember—the fruit or the fear?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They bring back word. They show the fruit. Notice: the facts are undeniable. All that follows—the crisis, the complaint, the consequence—flows not from false data, but from hearts that read the same signs differently.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their initial word is true: milk and honey flow there. The land is exactly as promised. This is how the report begins. Two voices will say the same truth and arrive at opposite conclusions.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But. However. Then they list the obstacles—strong peoples, fortified cities, giants. The south holds Amalek, the hills hold three nations, the coast and Jordan valley others. Every tribe of Canaan looms. They speak truth again, but leave God out of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Caleb's courage breaks through. 'Let us go up at once.' He quiets the people and speaks one true word: 'We are well able to overcome it.' He sees the same enemies, but he sees the Lord too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ten answer instantly, as if his faith threatens them. Fear moves faster than trust—it spreads like contagion. 'We aren't able.' They have already written the ending before the battle begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They call it an 'evil report.' Not evil for lying—the giants and giants truly exist—but evil for omitting God's power, for using truth as a weapon against faith. They see themselves as grasshoppers in their own sight, and that small sight becomes their prison.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in how quickly we too can speak truth while leaving God out—seeing real obstacles, real enemies, real weakness, but forgetting that we belong to the Lord who has already promised. The landscape hasn't changed; only our willingness to trust has.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
